Scalar equation refinements / v0.2 / 2026-10-11

The supplied Equation audit candidate.txt is evidence. Its proposed formulas
are checked within explicitly bounded models; its broader physical claims are
not computational conclusions. The following three implementations do not
convert SU(2) coefficients or ordinary complex amplitudes into finite fields.

API: globalThis.RusslRefinedScalar in the browser; CommonJS require of
src/refined-scalar.js returns the same immutable API.

Eq. 181: clebschGordan(j1,m1,j2,m2,J,M)
Returns coefficient, sign, exact squared rational (decimal numerator and
denominator strings), domain, phaseConvention, allowed, reason, kMin, kMax and
terms. j1,j2,J are exact integer/half-integer numbers from 0 through 6.
Magnetic numbers are exact integer/half-integer numbers. Out-of-multiplet,
magnetic-sum, triangle, integer-sum or magnetic-parity selection violations
return zero with allowed=false. Nonfinite, non-half-integer or excessive spin
inputs reject. An allowed coupling may also vanish by cancellation.

The completed Racah sum is the supplied Eq.181 with integer k ranging from
max(0,j2-J-m1,j1-J+m2) to min(j1+j2-J,j1-m1,j2+m2). Factorials and alternating
rational arithmetic use BigInt exactly. Only the final square root is binary
floating point. The phase is Condon-Shortley. This agrees with NIST's relation
between Clebsch-Gordan coefficients and Wigner 3j symbols and the finite
factorial sum:
https://dlmf.nist.gov/34.1.E1
https://dlmf.nist.gov/34.2.E4
https://dlmf.nist.gov/34.2.E5
https://docs.sympy.org/latest/modules/physics/wigner.html#sympy.physics.wigner.clebsch_gordan

The two phases in converting the DLMF 3j symbol to a CG coefficient cancel.
The remaining alternating sign is the explicit (-1)^k in the sum. For example,
the spin-half singlet has C(+1/2,-1/2)=+1/sqrt(2) and
C(-1/2,+1/2)=-1/sqrt(2). Domain: ordinary SU(2) angular-momentum coupling,
real coefficients used with complex amplitudes. No finite-field SU(2) or
p-adic interpretation is implemented or implied.

Eq. 318: arithmeticDelta(p,x)
Returns delta, input as normalized decimal string, residueModP2,
residueModP, unit, fermatQuotient (null for nonunits), exact and domain.
p is a prime integer from 2 through 97. x may be a decimal integer string of
at most 4096 digits, a safe integer number, or a bounded BigInt. Negative
integers are reduced to their canonical nonnegative residue modulo p^2.
Unsafe numeric inputs reject instead of silently rounding.

The implementation computes x^p modulo p^2 using exact BigInt modular
exponentiation, then divides the exactly p-divisible integer numerator and
reduces modulo p. This is delta_p(x)=(x-x^p)/p mod p on Z/p^2 Z. Choosing a
different representative of the same residue class leaves delta unchanged.
For units, q_p(x)=(x^(p-1)-1)/p mod p and delta_p(x)=-x q_p(x) mod p.
Nonunits have no Fermat quotient under that definition.

Eq.319 follows from substituting x^p=x-p delta_p(x) and y^p=y-p delta_p(y):
delta_p(xy)=x delta_p(y)+y delta_p(x) modulo p. Delta is not additive:
at p=2, delta(1)=0 while delta(1+1)=delta(2)=1. It is an arithmetic map
between residue rings, not an ordinary derivation on a finite field.

Cayley evolution: cayleyStep(H,state,dt,hbar=1)
H is a square Hermitian complex matrix with dimension 1 through 8 and state
has the same dimension. Complex values accept a real number, [re,im], or a
plain {re,im} object. All components are finite. The declared entries must
satisfy exact floating-point conjugate equality (including real diagonals);
the implementation does not silently symmetrize H. Entry magnitudes are at
most 1e6, the state Euclidean norm is at most 1e6, |dt| is at most 100,
hbar is finite and positive, and |dt H/(2 hbar)| per entry is at most 1e8.
These explicit numerical bounds prevent unchecked overflow and extreme
scaling. Scaled entries are computed directly, so zero or tiny H can remain
valid even when dt/(2 hbar) alone would overflow. Arrays must be dense plain
data arrays; accessors and extra properties reject without evaluation.
Caller-owned data are copied. The zero vector is allowed as a
linear-map input; it is not a normalized quantum state.

The conventional equation i hbar dpsi/dt=H psi uses
U=(I+i dt H/(2 hbar))^-1 (I-i dt H/(2 hbar)).
The candidate's opposite sign is the inverse-time step for the same
Hermitian H. It is not inherently nonunitary. The conventional step has
first-order change -i dt H psi/hbar. Both sign choices are unitary
mathematically when H is Hermitian and parameters are real as declared.

The implementation solves the complex linear system using partial-pivot
Gaussian elimination, not an explicit matrix inverse. It does not
renormalize the state. Returns state, Euclidean normBefore and normAfter,
normError, relativeNormError, absolute equation residual, relativeResidual,
tolerance, toleranceMet, renormalized=false, dimension, dt, hbar, domain and
the explicit convention. Relative residual is the backward-error ratio
||A psi_next-b||/(||A||_F ||psi_next||+||b||). Tolerance is 1e-10. A false
toleranceMet remains visible; it is not repaired by normalization or hidden
as a claim of exact floating-point norm conservation.

Verification scope
node --test tests/refined-scalar.test.cjs
Tests use the published SymPy examples, spin-half singlet/triplet values,
highest weights and singlet phases throughout the spin range, orthonormality
and completeness of integer and half-integer coupled bases, and a separate
standard-library Python DLMF 3j reference with exact Fraction arithmetic.
SymPy is absent from the available bundled and default Python installations;
an installed SymPy oracle was not run. This limitation is distinct from
comparison with values published in SymPy's official documentation.

Arithmetic tests compare exact integer powers, signed residues, units and
nonunits, representative independence, a nonadditivity counterexample and
Eq.319 over complete residue rings for p=2,3,5,7,11. Cayley tests cover
known diagonal phases, sigma-x, complex sigma-y, the first-order sign,
eight-dimensional inverse-time recovery, unnormalized-state norm retention,
finite bounds and non-Hermitian rejection. These tests verify algebra and
numerical models only, not the candidate's empirical physical assertions.
